name: Binge-eating disorder
summary: Recurrent episodes of eating unusually large amounts of food with loss of control, without regular compensatory behaviors. Psychotherapy (CBT) is first-line. Lisdexamfetamine is the only FDA-approved medication (adults, moderate to severe BED); no new eating-disorder drug approvals were found for 2024–2026.
plainSummary: People with binge-eating disorder often eat a lot of food quickly and feel out of control and upset afterward. Talk therapy helps most people, and one medicine is approved for adults.

approved.indication: Treatment of moderate to severe binge eating disorder (BED) in adults. Limitation of Use: not indicated or recommended for weight loss; safety and effectiveness for obesity not established.

dosing.notes: Severe renal impairment: max 50 mg/day; ESRD: max 30 mg/day. Avoid afternoon doses. Assess cardiac risk before starting.

boxedWarnings: Abuse, misuse, and addiction (risk of substance use disorder, overdose, and death)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to amphetamine products or other ingredients
MAOI use or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (including linezolid or IV methylene blue)
approved.plainSummary: A once-daily stimulant that can reduce the number of binge days in adults; it is a controlled medicine and is not meant for weight loss.

source.label: DailyMed: Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine dimesylate) capsules and chewable tablets

verified.note: Label effective 4/2026 checked (indication, BED dosing table, renal limits, contraindications).

offLabel.use: Reducing binge frequency, often with obesity
offLabel.notes: Placebo-controlled trials showed fewer binge episodes and weight loss, but discontinuation for adverse effects was higher (paresthesia, cognitive slowing, word-finding difficulty, kidney stones). Teratogenic risk (oral clefts) in pregnancy.

references.label: McElroy SL et al. Topiramate for BED associated with obesity: placebo-controlled study. Biol Psychiatry 2007 (PMID 17258690)
